newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine aide says progress in Russia Fleet talks.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine aide says progress in Russia Fleet talks.

text.p: Ukraine's top security official said on Thursday progress had been made with Moscow on settling a drawn-out row over the Black Sea Fleet but added that some people in Russia were trying to stop a deal being signed next week.

Volodymyr Horbulin, Secretary of the policy-making Security and Defence Council, said he had a "bad feeling" about plans for Russian President Boris Yeltsin to come to Kiev on May 30 and 31 for a visit which has been cancelled six times.

"A very active campaign has begun in Russian circles...aimed at breaking off President Boris Yeltsin's visit," said Horbulin, security aide to President Leonid Kuchma who visited Washington last week.

"Before the visit to the United States there was a warm hope that everything would be fine...Now I have a bad feeling. But we'll do our utmost to make this visit happen, without losing our dignity," he added.

In Moscow, Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky as saying plans for the visit were going full speed ahead and it would take place as planned -- though he said it was unclear what documents would be ready for signing.
Yeltsin's visit to sign a post-Soviet political deal has been held up by disagreements about the former Soviet Fleet, based at the Ukrainian port of Sevastopol in Crimea.
The two sides have agreed on how the fleet should be split but there has been tension over where the ships should be based.

Russia initially insisted on having only its ships in Sevastopol but Horbulin said the commanders of Russia's lion's share of the Fleet and Ukraine's naval commander had agreed that both countries could use the port.
"They agreed on bays... Undoubtedly progress has been made recently. Ukrainian ships will be in Sevastopol -- why shouldn't they? Sevastopol is a Ukrainian city," Horbulin said.
A defence ministry spokesman said technical details of the fleet had already been agreed in principle but what was needed was a political deal.
But Horbulin did not make clear what documents would be signed by Yeltsin -- if he came to Kiev at all. "I'll be very happy if he (Yeltsin) simply comes," he said.
Horbulin said it was not essential for a post-Soviet treaty to be signed at the same time as a deal on the fleet.

"Yeltsin said we would sign a treaty despite everything that was going on with the Black Sea fleet. He gave the order to solve this issue before his visit. But sometimes giving orders is easier than fulfilling them," he added.
Russia seized Crimea from the Ottoman empire in the 1780s and built the Sevastopol naval base almost immediately.

Soviet leader Nikita Krushchev then transferred Crimea to Ukraine in 1954. But Russian nationalists argue the move did not affect Sevastopol's special status as a town directly subordinate to Kremlin authorities.

Ukraine wants Yeltsin to sign a treaty recognising Ukraine's borders and its authority over Crimea, silencing politicians in Moscow who are apt to appeal to nationalist sentiment and historical claims to the peninsula.
